title: Your Coding Agent Wrote the Test. Who Checks It? with Donovan Brady
text: Your coding agent just wrote the test. Who checks it? Donovan Brady of Leapwork is back on TestGuild to answer the questions you sent in after our last episode. title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
text: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first not

title: From tester to engineering manager: Drew Pontikis on making the career change
text: Drew Pontikis fell into testing 16 or 17 years ago when an interviewer asked "can you code?" and he said no. Since then he has worked as a tester, test manager and quality lead, spent time in a communities of practice enablement team, and is now an engineering manager at Qflow, which builds data and sustainability software for the construction industry. He also helps run the MoTaverse engineering management chapter. Rosie and Drew talk about how TestBash Manchester in 2017 sparked his love of community, why his boss told him "your product is the team", and how a testing background prepares you for engineering management. Drew shares the engineering manager archetypes from Patrick Kua (technical, team, process and product focused) that shaped his MoTaCon workshop with Neil Younger and Parveen Khan, and how to work out which roles fit your shape. They also cover his approach to one-to-ones, staying true to your principles as a new manager, the "work vs gym" way of deciding when to use AI, and the idea of zero backlog.

title: Job title not found: careers beyond the label
text: Carol Batista is a senior QA engineer at Volkswagen Digital Hub in Barcelona. She started testing at 17 in her first year of engineering school in Fortaleza, Brazil, on a Lenovo project funded through a government tax deal with public universities. Fourteen years later, after roles at XING, a fintech startup and Bumble, she joins Rosie Sherry to talk about how quality careers are changing. They cover why going from manual testing to automation isn’t an “evolution” but a mix of skill sets, how Carol went from mentoring junior QAs at 21 to starting in Germany as an intern, and what happens to the industry if junior roles keep disappearing. Rosie shares her Venn diagram thinking on blending careers, and the pair talk about job titles, keyword filters, old-school CV uploads and the rise of vibe-coded portfolio pages. They also ask whether hiring should work more like dating, and try to name a role Carol would love: someone who connects testers across projects so learnings aren’t lost. Staff engineer, quality coach and QA architect all make the shortlist. Highlights include: Starting at 17: How a tax-relief deal between the Brazilian government and big tech put Carol on a Lenovo testing project in her first year of college. From test analyst to intern: Mentoring junior QAs at 21, then moving to Hamburg through a visa-sponsored internship. Experience over education: Why practice and opportunity matter as much as qualifications, and how to reach college students in uncertain times. Blending careers: Rosie’s Moment, Venn diagrams of the MoT team, and whether generalists are becoming specialists again. Job titles and hiring: Quality engineer as the most popular title in the MoTaverse, and the contrast between hiring at Volkswagen and Bumble. Portfolios and profiles: Vibe-coded portfolio pages, bot versions of yourself, and using your MoT profile, stars and badges as career data. Hiring like dating: Matching on skills and affinity rather than job titles and keywords. The connector role: Carol’s dream job, and whether to call it staff engineer, quality coach or QA architect.

title: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?
author: redleathercouch
text: I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code. What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me. I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins. I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great. Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...). Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.
